title: Vav
hook: a hook, and the word "and": it joins things

segments.voice: Yesterday, a breath added to two names, and Abram and Sarai became Abraham and Sarah. Your line was heh is breath. Whose name did you say slowly? Today, a letter that holds things together. Day one thousand three hundred thirty-four.

In the book of Exodus, Moses is given building instructions for the Tabernacle, the tent where God's presence would dwell among the people. The list is detailed: boards, sockets, curtains of blue and purple and scarlet. And somewhere in that list, a tiny, practical part. Something has to hold the curtain up. The pillars get hooks of gold, and the curtain hangs on them. Nobody comes to see the hooks. But without them a beautiful curtain is a heap of cloth on the floor. The Hebrew word for those hooks is the name of today's letter.
screen: `BUILDING THE TABERNACLE.` → `CURTAINS OF BLUE AND SCARLET.` → `HOOKS OF GOLD.`

segments.voice: Vav. Three things hang on this little hook. The first is the word. In the Torah's instructions for the Tabernacle, the hooks on the pillars are vavim, the plural of vav. The King James puts it plainly: "their hooks shall be of gold." And the letter looks the part: a single upright stroke with a small bend at the top, like a peg on a wall. The second is a job. In Hebrew, the word "and" isn't a separate word at all. It's this letter, clipped onto the front of the next word. Ve. Hooked on. Open the first chapter of Genesis in Hebrew and you can watch it work, sentence after sentence. The King James keeps many of the hooks: "And God said, Let there be light: and there was light." Each part of creation is fastened to the one before it, and the story never lets go of the thread. The third is a surprise. Vav doesn't only connect words. Sometimes it stops being a consonant and carries a vowel instead, an o or an oo. In shalom, the o you hear in the middle is held up by a vav. So the letter that joins sentences also joins sounds, letting the consonants around it ring. That's the whole character of vav: it's rarely the point of the sentence, and the sentence falls apart without it. Out in a working day, a lot of good work looks like that. The person who introduces two friends. The text that says, I'll come with you. A small and, that keeps two things from falling apart.
screen: `VAVIM: HOOKS OF GOLD.` · `"AND" IS A LETTER, HOOKED ON.` · `AND GOD SAID… AND THERE WAS.` · `VAV CARRIES A VOWEL TOO.` · then, large: `RARELY THE POINT. ALWAYS HOLDING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find two things that should be joined. Settle, and breathe. Look around your life for two things sitting apart that belong together. Two friends who'd like each other. A family member and a phone call. A good intention and the first small step. Your morning and a moment of quiet. Don't fix anything yet. Just let the word "and" sit between them. This, and that. Feel what it would take to hook them together. If you pray, you can bring both of them into your prayer at once. The bell holds the time.
Vav. A hook, like the gold hooks of the Tabernacle; the letter that means and, and sometimes carries a vowel. Today's word.
Your line: vav connects. Today, join the two things you named: make the introduction, send the message, take the first step. Day one thousand three hundred thirty-four.

howItsDone: Children learning Hebrew may meet vav early, both as a letter and as the prefix ve-, 'and'; readers of the Hebrew Bible hear it at the start of verse after verse in the stories of Genesis.

notes: Exodus 26:32 and Genesis 1:3 quoted from the KJV (1769), allowed for this path; a Keeper may prefer JPS 1917 wording.
Hook summarizes Exodus 26:31–32 (veil hung on pillars with gold hooks, vavim); 'the most beautiful curtain in the camp' is narrative color, not a claim from the text. Confirm or soften.
'The King James keeps every hook it can' is a loose description; it does not translate every vav as 'and'. Keeper may prefer 'keeps many of them'.
Vav as a vowel letter (holam male, shuruk) and the o in shalom: standard grammar; confirm phrasing.
Letter shape described as an upright stroke with a small bend at the top; confirm.
